title: Warming up for concerts like an athlete
summary: Leeman explains he arrives two hours early to warm up his hands and feet with exercises and caffeine, comparing drumming to athletics.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: I warm up without anything but caffeine. And that's coffee -- and I get there two hours early, and all the concerts I do across the country, I am whipped if I don't and, we'd get into towns, and we'd get off the plane with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and I go and I have it

all set up, somebody check me in, I'm going over to the hall, four o'clock in the afternoon, we're there from the plane, the concert is from 8 to 10 and I'm over there at 4 o'clock with my own coffee pot I travel with and my change of clothes, and I sit down backstage and I practice, and I warm up, rather, is the word. I don't practice, I don't do any of those things. I never touch a drum; I have a set of exercises, and I'd be happy to show anybody that was interested.

And I could warm my hands and my feet, you know, because more than any other instrument, playing drums is a great deal of athletics. You never saw an Olympic field, they don't get there early before they do their hurdles, they warm up, and if they want to swim, they're gonna warm up. No matter what you do that's athletic, you got to warm up those muscles, you got to pull something.
And that's what I have to do. Play the drums without any stimulants, any false stimulants.
So I'm getting wound up in this thing, but that's it. You asked me a question, and I don't need any stimulants.
Sounds beautiful. We can end this for now. (CUT)
